about: Benchmarks for programs that help people get public benefits or file taxes. Every number here is a default, never a fact. Each entry lists the published points behind it, with source, link, year, and place, and says what it does not cover. Any chain file can override any entry by giving its own low, likely, and high. An entry with a step field is the default range a page holds that step against.

benchmarks.label: Share of people sent outreach who respond
benchmarks.how_set: Low and high are the lowest and highest of the four points below. Likely is the midpoint of the two middle points.
benchmarks.does_not_cover: Outreach of any kind other than a letter, a text, an email, or a public launch. The four points reach very different groups. Older adults in Pennsylvania by mail, people in Los Angeles who had already applied for SNAP, and taxpayers in twelve states who could use a new federal filing tool. The Los Angeles group had already applied, so it responds far more often than a cold list. Some people who started the federal filing checker lived outside the pilot states, so that point runs high against its own base.

points.what: Started the eligibility checker of a free federal tax filing tool, against the IRS research division's estimate of 19 million eligible taxpayers. More than 3.3 million started it, printed as 3,340,500 in Figure 2.
points.source: Internal Revenue Service, IRS Direct File Pilot Program, Filing Season 2024 After Action Report, Publication 5969
points.measured: IRS system counts against an IRS estimate of the eligible population

points.what: Called the number on an outreach letter about SNAP, letter and reminder postcard only. The raw call rate.
points.source: Finkelstein and Notowidigdo, Take-Up and Targeting, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2019, Table II
points.year: Letters mailed in 2016, calls counted over seven months
points.place: Pennsylvania, adults 60 and over on Medicaid and not on SNAP
points.measured: Call logs, lottery study, 5,314 people mailed

points.what: Called the number on an outreach letter about SNAP that offered phone help to apply.
points.source: Finkelstein and Notowidigdo, Take-Up and Targeting, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2019, Table II
points.year: Letters mailed in 2016, calls counted over seven months
points.place: Pennsylvania, adults 60 and over on Medicaid and not on SNAP
points.measured: Call logs, lottery study, 10,629 people mailed

points.what: Called a new phone line at least once before the deadline, after a text or email saying they could do their required SNAP interview at a time of their choosing.
points.source: Giannella, Homonoff, Rino, and Somerville, Administrative Burden and Procedural Denials, working paper, April 2023
points.place: Los Angeles County, California, applicants through one online application
points.measured: Call records for the treatment group, lottery study, 64,798 applications

benchmarks.label: Share of people who responded who go on to start
benchmarks.how_set: Low and high are the lowest and highest of the three points below. Likely is the middle one.
benchmarks.does_not_cover: Any step but the first real start, an application or a sign-in. The federal filing tool turned many people away at the checker on purpose, because the tool did not fit their taxes, so its point runs low for a reason that is not a failure. Phone help with the application roughly doubles the start rate over a letter alone in the one study that tested both.

points.what: Signed in to a free federal tax filing tool, of those who started its eligibility checker. 423,450 signed in, of 3,340,500 who started.
points.source: Internal Revenue Service, IRS Direct File Pilot Program, Filing Season 2024 After Action Report, Publication 5969, Figure 2

points.what: Applied for SNAP, of those who called the number on a letter and postcard with no phone help.
points.source: Finkelstein and Notowidigdo, Take-Up and Targeting, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2019, Table II
points.year: Letters mailed in 2016, followed nine months
points.place: Pennsylvania, adults 60 and over on Medicaid and not on SNAP
points.measured: State application records and call logs, lottery study

points.what: Applied for SNAP, of those who called the number on a letter that offered phone help to apply.
points.source: Finkelstein and Notowidigdo, Take-Up and Targeting, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2019, Table II
points.year: Letters mailed in 2016, followed nine months
points.place: Pennsylvania, adults 60 and over on Medicaid and not on SNAP
points.measured: State application records and call logs, lottery study

benchmarks.label: Share of people who started who finish
benchmarks.how_set: Low and high are the lowest and highest of the three points below. Likely is the middle one.
benchmarks.does_not_cover: Finishing anything longer than one application, one return, or one interview, such as a training program. Two of the three points come from the same federal filing tool, measured two ways. The Los Angeles point counts callers who stayed on the line at least five minutes, which the authors call a conservative floor for the time an interview takes, not a count of finished interviews.

points.what: Had a return accepted, of those who signed in to a free federal tax filing tool. 140,803 accepted returns, of 423,450 who signed in.
points.source: Internal Revenue Service, IRS Direct File Pilot Program, Filing Season 2024 After Action Report, Publication 5969, Figure 2

points.what: Submitted a return, of those who started one in a free federal tax filing tool. 161,042 submitted, of 395,483 who started a return.
points.source: Internal Revenue Service, IRS Direct File Pilot Program, Filing Season 2024 After Action Report, Publication 5969, Figure 2

points.what: Stayed on the line at least five minutes, of SNAP applicants who called a new phone line to do their required interview.
points.source: Giannella, Homonoff, Rino, and Somerville, Administrative Burden and Procedural Denials, working paper, April 2023
points.place: Los Angeles County, California, applicants through one online application
points.measured: Call records for the treatment group, lottery study, 64,798 applications

benchmarks.label: Share of everyone offered help who enrolled and would not have enrolled anyway
benchmarks.how_set: Low and high are the lowest and highest of the three points below. Likely is the middle one.
benchmarks.does_not_cover: Anything but SNAP. Each figure is measured over everyone offered the help, not only the people who used it, so it is never multiplied by reach or uptake. Two very different groups, older adults in Pennsylvania reached by mail and online applicants in Los Angeles reached by text. The Los Angeles group had already applied before it was offered help, so in a chain its point belongs to the people who started, not to everyone at the start. A program that reaches people who are harder to enroll, or easier, will land outside this range.

points.what: A letter plus phone help with the application. 17.6 percent enrolled within nine months against 5.8 percent of the comparison group.
points.source: Finkelstein and Notowidigdo, Take-Up and Targeting, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2019, Table II
points.year: Letters mailed in 2016, followed nine months
points.place: Pennsylvania, adults 60 and over on Medicaid and not on SNAP
points.measured: State enrollment records, lottery study, 10,629 offered and 10,630 in the comparison group

points.what: A letter and a reminder postcard with no phone help. 10.5 percent enrolled against 5.8 percent.
points.source: Finkelstein and Notowidigdo, Take-Up and Targeting, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2019, Table II
points.year: Letters mailed in 2016, followed nine months
points.place: Pennsylvania, adults 60 and over on Medicaid and not on SNAP
points.measured: State enrollment records, lottery study, 5,314 offered and 10,630 in the comparison group

points.what: A text or email telling online applicants they could call for their required interview at a time of their choosing. The gain in ever receiving SNAP, five months out.
points.source: Giannella, Homonoff, Rino, and Somerville, working paper, April 2023
points.year: Applications from October 2020 to May 2021, followed five months
points.place: Los Angeles County, California, applicants through one online application

benchmarks.label: SNAP dollars a newly enrolled household receives in a year
benchmarks.how_set: Each point is a printed average monthly benefit times twelve. Low and high are the lowest and highest of the three. Likely is the middle one.
benchmarks.does_not_cover: Households with children, who receive far more. Anyone under 60. Any year but 2016, with no adjustment for inflation or for later changes to benefit levels. People a program newly brings in tend to receive less than people who enroll on their own, which is why the low end sits where it does. Benefits are money moved to a household from the federal government, not new wealth.

points.what: Enrollees who got a letter plus phone help. Printed as $101.32 a month.
points.source: Finkelstein and Notowidigdo, Take-Up and Targeting, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2019, Table IV
points.measured: State benefit records, enrollees within nine months

points.what: Enrollees who got a letter only. Printed as $115.38 a month.
points.source: Finkelstein and Notowidigdo, Take-Up and Targeting, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2019, Table IV
points.measured: State benefit records, enrollees within nine months

points.what: Enrollees in the comparison group, who enrolled with no outreach. Printed as $145.94 a month.
points.source: Finkelstein and Notowidigdo, Take-Up and Targeting, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2019, Table IV
points.measured: State benefit records, enrollees within nine months
